The Emperor angelfish, Pomacanthus imperator, exhibits several distinct life-history traits that have been documented across its range. Newly hatched larvae are remarkably small, with a freshly emerged individual weighing just 0.00011 grams [Wwb = just 0.00011 grams]. This minuscule size is typical of pelagic marine teleosts and reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent development. Following a planktonic larval phase and a dramatic metamorphosis, juveniles settle onto coral reefs, where they begin a period of rapid somatic growth. Field surveys suggest that under typical environmental conditions, including a stable water temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], the maximum lifespan of the species reaches approximately 5110 days [am = approximately 5110 days], placing it among the longer-lived members of the pomacanthid family. This extended longevity is thought to be linked to its relatively slow life pace and the high survival rates characteristic of large, territorial reef fishes.

The onset of reproductive capability during the juvenile-to-adult transition is marked by the attainment of a specific body length. Sexual maturation occurs once individuals reach a standard length of 19.2 centimeters [Lp = 19.2 centimeters], a size that likely corresponds to the minimum structural requirements for successful gonadal development. This length at puberty is comparatively modest relative to the species' ultimate size, allowing individuals to begin the transition to maturity well before they have ceased somatic growth. Growth trajectories derived from mark-recapture studies indicate that the ultimate standard length, representing the maximum size a fully grown adult can achieve, is 41.2 centimeters [Li = 41.2 centimeters]. Reaching this asymptotic length involves a deceleration in growth rate as metabolic resources are increasingly channeled toward maintenance and, eventually, toward reproductive effort in the mature adult phase.

Reproductive output in P. imperator has been quantified through both laboratory observations of captive pairs and field-based estimates from gravid females. At the species' typical thermal regime of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], females achieve a maximum daily spawning rate that corresponds to an annual output of roughly 540000 eggs per year. This high fecundity, characteristic of many pelagic-spawning reef fishes, is partitioned across numerous spawning events throughout the extended breeding season, with each event releasing a moderate number of buoyant eggs. The corresponding maximum reproductive rate, when expressed on an annual basis, amounts to approximately 540000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 540000 eggs per year]. This substantial yearly production helps offset the high levels of egg and larval mortality typical of the planktonic environment, ensuring that at least a small fraction of offspring survive to settlement.

Body mass parameters further define the life-history strategy of this species. The ultimate wet weight, or the largest body mass recorded in fully grown, reproductively active adults, stands at 2852 grams [Wwi = 2852 grams]. This considerable mass, achieved over years of sustained feeding on a diet of sponges, tunicates, and other benthic invertebrates, anchors the species among the larger members of its genus. The contrast between the minute birth weight of 0.00011 grams [Wwb = 0.00011 grams] and the adult mass of 2852 grams [Wwi = 2852 grams] is striking, representing an approximately 26-million-fold increase in wet mass over the course of the individual's life. Such a pronounced size disparity underscores the critical importance of the juvenile growth phase, during which the majority of somatic mass is accumulated before the onset of sexual maturity.

Comparisons with the closely related Cortez angelfish, Pomacanthus zonipectus, provide additional context for the Emperor angelfish's growth parameters. In P. zonipectus, standard length at puberty occurs at roughly 46.7 percent of the ultimate length, a proportional relationship that appears to be conserved in P. imperator given its measured length at puberty of 19.2 centimeters [Lp = 19.2 centimeters] relative to an ultimate length of 41.2 centimeters [Li = 41.2 centimeters]. Annual fecundity of approximately 540000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 540000 eggs per year] reflects a classic trade-off between investment per offspring and total reproductive output, balancing egg size against total clutch frequency over the breeding season.
